div.head: MURDIR AT DURHAM.
div.p: THE MURDIR AT DURHAM.

An arrest has been made by the police who have been appointed to inquire into the details of die shocking murder which was perpetrated at Bellmont, a farm lying between Blanchland and Stool, pe, Durham, on the evening of the Ist inst. The farm, it will be rememberwl, is situate in a wild and lonely part of the muntry, and a good distance Crone any habitat... The occupier of the farm was Robert Snowdon, who lived alone with his father, an old man over seventy years of age, and a servant girl or housekeeper, named Jane Barron. About live o'clock in the evening Robert Snowdon went out with a lighted candle into enrol the outhouses to do some work, but did not return. The housekeeper shortly afterwards went into the byre to milk the comb and on her return she said she had men blood dropping from the loft above, through the ceiling. The old man remarked that they had been killing sheep, and that it would be from them ihat the blood was running. During the night they- ung man did not return, and the next morning the housekeeper went to milk again, and mid , she noticed the blood BIM corning through the left boards , into the byre, in greater quantities thee on the previous I night. Together with the deceased's father she went into , the room above the byre, and then the body of the deceased, 1. lying inn pool of blood, W. discovered. The hick part of , his head had beer knocked in, the whole of the front teeth 1 were knocked out, and there was a deep cut on the chin. A large hammer was lying near the body covered with blood, I , with which the deed hot been apparently committed. The person who hoe been arrested by the police is the hence-, keeper, Jane Ban on, end the tumour that Mr. Snowdon, had also been arrosted on inc ,rrect, there being no evidence , againet hint to warrant such a course of action. When charged in the usual manner the woman Barron at first I turned slightly pile, but her face exhibited not the least sign of emotion or guilt. Sheet first returned no answer to the charge, but after about a minute's reflmtion she replied that shewas not guilty. The deceased and his father bad long borne the reputation of being "curious folks," but the neigh- I boursappear to know little or nothing about their mode of life. The murdered man's mother died about six weeks ago, pod it in related that, when the doctor had given up all hopes of herrecovety, deceased went to one of the neighbours' houses, I and askpd if any of the occupants knew anything about the "laying out" of dead bodies, as the "old woman " went going to die. Upon being answered in the negative, he re- ' marked that he and his father would have to manage as best they could themselves. flit added that he constructed the I coffin in the very apartment in which he was afterwards murdered. When Dr. Montgomery had men the youngman's body on thespot where it was found, he appear;to hive given ! permission to, old Mr. Snoirdon and the woman Barone to I remove it into the house. If hie they did, andwlien the police arrived they found the corpse washed clean, and the stains of blood he., removed (min the flooring of the byre, the old man having.as he himself said, moiled it up. 'Mr. Snowdon also stated that lie had " dumped " the blood I and water on the midden,md upon searching there the police ' , found mme of deceased's Meth, together with evident traces of blood upon a piece -4 boarding. In the byre also wm found the imprint of a bloody hand, while in the house the police discovertd a dress belonging to Barroa which was .ound to be stained with blood in several places, the imide lof thepocket !wing smeared as if 0 hand dripping with blood I had been intreducedinto it. This fact however, ill scarcely I tell against the accused, as it might have been done after Dr. Montgomery had given permission for the removal of , I the corpse.

Kenyon, of Warrington, writing on Lord Derby's , recent speeetiPat II odde-sdeld, enc. —Though it is always a pleasure to read the speeches of his Lordship, I differ from JI the iamence he derives from the return. of income tax, the 'l' deposits in savings hanks, and tam consumption of tea. Ido not think the return of income tax is to 114 relied upon a• ' acetrately indicating the prosperity of the country, for ,1 whilst in tirnes of prosperity it may be considerably under- estimated, iu times of depression 1 believe that very many : pay on considerably more than they make. I know a large number who did so last year; and, with reference to the de. , posits in savings banks, I fancy during last year there ho been. considerable amount deposited therein which in more prosperous years would have been otherwise invested. And , I think, with regard to, the larger consumption of tea, that loony have taken it to help It meal, who at other timee I have been al,k to obtain something. tcore nourishing and better. It is necessary that our stahums should be really i accurate, and to duly consieer, the circumstances under which they haoe been obtained, and the causes which hovel influenced them, before we can arrive at any correct con- , elusions from them. Bad thoes, with low prices, are al- i ways good for those who have • hued income, and the years 1877 and 1878 were very good years for the landed proprie- tors, for though their rents might not increase, they could obtain considerably more of nearly every article for the same amount of cash. I think the very large number of failures during the net year or two, and the very small divi. j dends paid by large, and until recently prosperous linos, are tn.ro to be relied upon as ietdicoriee7 the prosperity or other.; wise of the manufacturing. commercial, and industrial core.l moody. I very moch Admire his Lordship's remarks in I reterence to the military system of the Continent. -1.0 me I it seems very desirable that we should accurately understand and realise the position we he'd in regard to other countries as a manufacturing and commercial people, for it is only by so doing that we moo make the best of it.

SATURDAY, JANUARY 17, 1680.

THE DISTRESS IN WESTERN IRELAND. Lain week the Lord Mayor of London addressed a circular to the Mayors of the chief towns thriughout the kingdom calling upon them to co-operate with him in raising funds to relieve the people in the dis- tressed districts of Ireland. There can be no doubt that the state of affairs is rapidly growing worm in the sister island, and the voluntary aubacriptians to 'the Duchene of Marlboroush's food" are not coming ! in quite as freely as wan expected. The reason of this 1 in mid to be that a come quarter+ disaatisfaction has I Seen felt at the send-official manner of the Duchess's ! appeal. It is a matter of notoriety that the wife of the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland wan acting under the 1 instructiona of the Government, and there has been • 1 vague uspicion in some quarters that the appeal to • ,1 certain extent was a party more. To say the least of 1 it, it it rather unfortunate that Lord Beaconsfield ahould have designed a mode of raising a relief fund 1 that hoe about it some appearance of deception. One of the consequences IA that there are now in Ireland three or four separate funds for the relief of the distresei The daughter-in-law of the Duke of Aber• corn haa started a •• Marchionesa of Hamilton's fund," and in addition to the " Duchess of Marlborough's fund" there is the " Lord Mayor's fund,' and we believe • "land League fund," which the Home Rulers purpose to raise on their own isecount. The Lord Mayor of London's subecription list opened at the Mansion House is an auxiliary to the "Duchess of Marlborough's fund." At Warrington, St. Helens, and other places, the Mayor, have thin week remised a telegram from the Lord Mayor of Dublin stating that "argent need exists for aid to preserve the Biala poor from famine," and the first response is the announcement that collections will be made to. morrow (Sunday) in several of the churches and chapels at Warrington. The money no raised will, we take it, be remitted to the Lord Mayor of Dublin whose relief fund in, as we have intimated, one altogether separate from that of the Tracheas of Marlborough, and which some will continue to regard to a certain, xtent in the light of a " Government fund." It is as well that these distinctions should be known, inasmuch as the question may be shortly 1 before Town Cauncilsand other local authorities as to ! 1 whether immediatentepsahould not be taken to get up AO ! Irish Fatnine Relief Fund. Into whatever channel !the money no raised may be directed we do not for moment doubt that it will be applied to the hest advantage in the relief of this terrible distress.

It must be admitted on all sides that the news from ; the western districts of Ireland is sad and grevona in the extreme. Thee, • is no :ack of full and reliable accounts either; for the Central News Association, • and several d -illy metropolitan Olken., have their I special correspondent, in different parts of the dia- ; teemed dietricts, and the reports they give all concur ; in the one terrible f int that thousands of men, women, ' and children, scantiiy clad and In housed, will be left , without either f vol or fire during this severe winter weather if opeedly succour be not afforded. It is ; the genuine Keltic peasantry of the western sea board front Donegal to Kerry, that the unprecedentedly culd'and wet summer ;which has more or less injured the agricultural populations all over the kingdom) has brought to the brink of actual famine. These poor people are Jeacribod as utterly helpless, inasmuch as they have; lost, by no immediate fault of their own, all that they had to depend on for the winter's suste- nance. Their potatoes are gone, and there wag no sun during the last summer to enable them to dry their peat or turf, on which lone they have to de- pend for fuel. To supply a whole population over large tract of country remote from railway stations, with fuel, is no easy matter, and yet from all aocounta it would appear that a supply of coal to districts where the peat has not been secured, is quite as necessary as food. The terrible picture whi• h is to-day brought before the charitable and well to-d people throughout the whole of the empire is this' of a large rural population, men, women, and little children in despair at the approach of a terrible in- fliction, and from which by no mere effort of their own can they peseibly eadape. It ought to be enough to make known the fact that within leas than a day's , journey from the capital of this great empire, the rural population of at least four large counties are in danger of perishing from cold and huniser , is coder to, reduce a sufkisnt -um to plo., tLess ob. fortunate peopl.• out of the reach of danger. We believe that timely relief sad' be ailordesL yet would • venture to remind those in authority, and all those who have the power of giving, that k • 'let qoi , dial, and from all aeconnui there is nu time to be lost. It would be a baiting disgrace if i; stionld happen . it did happen nearly five and thirty years ago, at the time of the first great pots toe famine—that a rapid increase should be obeerved to take place in the mortality returns, and that inaolated cases should begin to be reported of ' death from starvation" ant death from " exyaire,"
Whaseves objeastuae may tpe felt that the ooarse',

which the Government has taken in this matter, both the Dirchees of Marlborough's Food, and the Lord Mayor of Dublin', Food, am o.t of sheer kindness st.d c.,:pa-sX•11 (.1 'offering humanity, any one may srea ppnf. In Ir land there is always a j,alous on ,•f p pie, that the dis- tribution of relit.f of this kind may be taken advantage of for proselyrbing purpose. But there is no fear of such being the case in this instant, inasmuch no the Executive Committee of the Duche.a's fund cunaiata in equal proportions of Roman Crthelie nod Proton- taut Indict, and every po.dble precaution has been tab, wriinst Inct intrusion of anything in the ithape id sec arienism. That the Lord Mayor's fund will be distributed with equal judgnent sod impartiality no reasonable person can entertain ndoubt.

Gramme Cexxsz.—Writing friana Congleton, eeoc. reepondent of the Grorer says :—"Poe acme time past the Cheshire dairy fanners have been doing very badly, and have been complaining bitterly about their unpleasant position. At one time their cheese woe a drug in the market, and prices reached an unprecedentydly low level. Few of them were able to hold on in hopes of higher rates. For nne thiug, they wanted money; for another, they now make cheese more for immediate consumption than for keeping purposos. They make butter as well as cheese, and use up their cream tor the Mitten The qualityof the cheese perhaps suffers in consequence. But now the Cheshire farmers are doing a great deal hatter th.tn they were, the higher prices which they have been no long expecting are practically realMml. I need not go into deMils chewing how cheese has latelo ad- vanced this information ia given so fully in your journal that your readers are thoroughly acquainted with the mat- ter. But, as showing the extent of the recent rice, it may be mentioned that Cheshirecheese which a short time ago did not fetch more than 40s. now realisee gate 703., and consequently the fanners' prospects (and purseslare far more satinfactory than they were. There has been also a good deal of speculation in the article, and certain people have made large sums of money. They certainly deserve this for their power of divining what was going to happen with re gard to the price of cheese." ORDER ow rex BONS or TEMERRANCE, CHESHIRE DIVISION.—On Monthly last the half-yearly meeting of the Cheshire Grand DIVIAOII of die Order of Sons of Temperance was held in the Mechanics' Institute, Crewe. There was a numerous attendance of representatives from the several nub- ordin.tte divisious in Oie district, comprising Runcorn, Crewe. Chester, Handley, Winaford, and Northwich, also a full at- tendance of officere. The meeting was opened at 10.30 a.m. by Brother George Cooke, G.W.P., who congratulated the repre.ntatives on their continued iuterest in the welfare of the order, and expressed the plersure it afforded him to are so many present, as be believed they had all come together RR the one great purpose, via., that of discussing the im- portant business of the Order. They hoped by united efforts I. devise the hest means to advance its career of usefulness and prospe.ity, and to nuccessf ally propagate itt noble prin- ciples throughout all the towns and villages of Cheshire. Bro. Joseph Bowering, P.G.W.P , nth! Il clroe,t !!.....=tya be remembered that each officer and metnber of the "grand division" was responsible for the meccas or otherwiee of the institution,:tqd that each ond should consider it his especial duty to eadrt bra utmoet influence to this end in his own suMmlinate division. Too much importanne emit, not be attached to individual effort. Bro. Thos. Cooke, G Scribe, in his report, stated that the increase in membership during the past half-year had been very satisfactory. The fund, of society were in a moat flourishing cendition, as there had not been a death throughout the district during the last eleven months. This spoke well for teetotalism. He urged upon each present to be up and doing during the new year upon which we had just entered, and with a firmer determion- tion than ever to fight manfully and energetically for the further extension of temperance principles. M'Cullooh, of Liverpool, crane,:—" The renewed inquiry with which the year opened has been followed by considerable activity in chemicals, with an increasing demand both for home trade anti export. A further advance has been established in soda ash, caustic smla, and bleaching powder. There has been more denire to porch.° for delivery over the year, and • very large business would have been done bat for the higher prices asked. 'l'lrr tone of the trade generally is better More doing in alum, chlorate of potash, tartaric acid, borax, of ammonia. Arsenic is better. Zlitrate of smia maintains int price. Tartars are scarce and firm, and there is more inquiry for manganese. Phosphate materials are dull."—We quote the following from .1. Berger Spence and' Cu's weekly report, dated London, January 10th ,—“The opening week of the new year has been quite aatisfactory,i from a 'amines* point of view, for chemicaln. Although I the full tiae of operations is hardly near yet resumed, there I, little of evidence of an active month likely to follow. Inquiries are numerous, and apparently genuine. The de.; m inds for expolt rather increase than otherwise. and sales are being made in anticipation of an early opening of the ice-bound ports. The reqoirements for the home trade also are larger, an.l constmers become more and more convinced that the improvement it winething more than the spasmodic speculativenena they were at first disposed to reord it. As • consequence there is awleoegdioprr,ilion la buy for stock as a safe investment for capital. There in more anxiety evinged in regard to the question of forward supplies, nego- tiations for contracts therefore increasing. Makers as a role have hut limited supplies to offer for immediate delivery, and prices contioe firm. Coterie soda is in rather larger demand, and somewhat ecarce in supply. Aah is firm, and active. Bleaching powder is in good request for both prompt and forward delivery, aod parcels offering find a ready market. Acetates are nostained with tolerable steeliness. Acids show rather less firmness. Metallic salts alno, if any- thing, are a shade easier. Minerals continue to develop satisfactory nymptoms of improvement, and an extended business is being done in nearly every item The 1110 E at- tention is of course being attracted by iron ore, the demand for which increoen weekly to a very considerable extent. The raphl increane in the value of good English ore is in- cluding the itnportation of foreign descriptions on an ex- tensive wale. Metal, The northern pig iron trade con- firm.. M a condition of persistent ulvance. The new year ban been ushered in by a further inereme of demand on foreign account, and this, combined with the favourahle position in which makers now are generally, bee given an additional stimulus to the trade."

MINIM' We°. en Laracoamac. An adjourned conference of miners' delegates was held on Monday at the Miners' Hall. Wigan, to consider the wages question and re- plies of the masters to the notice by the men for an ad- vance in wages equal to the last reduction. Mr. W. Pickard, of Wigan, presided, and delegates were present from the varions mining districts in Lanmtshire, representing abont 20,000 men. Deputations from the men having waited upon the masters at the end of last week, the replies thee received were reported to Monday's conference. The great propor- lion of the replies was to the effect that prices had not sufficiently increased to justify any advance in wagen at present, hut come of the masters stated that they would give the advance if other masters granted it. The conference was engaged for six hours di:mussing what steps should he taken by the men, and ultimately it ream resolved that, "Seeing that the employers refuse legion an advance of wages, on account of their not having in- creased the price of coal, but hold out a hope that they will be thle to give it towards the end of the preant month, we adjourn tide meeting for three weeks, and in The event of the employers not giving the desired advance or consenting ton basis for a sliding scale toy that time, we adopt means to decrease the output of coal until they do so." The con- ference also remlved to organise committees in the whole of the principal mining districts, and to hold mass ineetings of colliers there in order to carry out the above resolution, and to take steps for the eucceseful working of the slitting scale. should one beadopted by the masters and men. A large meeting of miners in the St. Helens district was held on Tuesday night, in the Old Mill large assembly room, St. Helens. Mr. Piggott. of A. Helens, presided. After the deleg, nylon attended the conference bad given their report, Mr. W. Pickard, of Wigan. was called mum to address the meoting He commenced by reading over the resolutions as mimed at the conference, and then reviewed the position of the coal trade, and the state nf work oen's wages, and appealed to the meeting for an exprrosion of opinion ado whether the conference was not justified in coming ts the conclusion adopted on Monday. The meeting was unani- mous in its approval of the course taken at the conference, and votes of thanks were passed to Mr. Pickard and other friends who had addressed the assembly. His I efforts bid fair to succeed. The.objects of this society are I philanthropic, and on a similar scale to other benefit societies I existing in the neighbourhood. By the payment of a small I weekly subscription, the members or their famili. become I entitled at death to receive £lO In the case of a man, Ed in the case of a woman, and, in a corresponding ratio, on the death of ttnir children. div.p: THE F VrAL ACCIDENT TO A MAN AT MI.SSRS ILSPRATT'S, WIDNES.

THE INQUEST.' CM Monday an inquest was held by Mr. Barker, deputy- coroner, at the Slersey Hotel, Money-road, Widnes, on the body of John Riley. aged 24, a contractor's labourer, of ye,idiebary, near Manchester, who was killed on the previous Friday, w.hilst asnisting to put up an acid cistern at the works of Messrs Muspralt and Co., Anne-street.—The Coro- ner said, considering the evidence the witnesses would give, it appeared to him that the deoeaaed bad met with his death accidentally. He did not see that anyone was to blame but Kelly, a man assisting deceased, who had neglected to put in a certain wedge but there had md been that gross negli- gence on his part which would make hint criminally respon- sible. He could not, therefore, think that they could re.ura any each verdict as one of manslaughter. There was no dohbt that if Kelly could have prevented the accident he would h.ive done so. so as to keep himself train being in- jure.l.—.lan, dec-ased's brother, stated that he ! came to Work at Messrs Mneprates on the Thorn- ' day before the accident. He identitiesl the body lying at the dead-house as that of his brother.— Peter Scrvingeour said he wan a contractor, and on the !previous Friday he was engaged in putting up an acid stone cistern at Messrs. Masprates. She deceased was acting an one of his hmourers. Three of the foot stones of which the cistern was formed were fixed in their places, being Deo sides and an end one, and the deceased was &sedating in arranging them when the accident happened. Ile (whom) was away at the time. hiving gone for some inslia rubber for the joints. this being use only thing which would stand the acid. When he returned, it would be about a quarter past eleven. and he found the deceased and another man under one of the side stones. The men had been acing a crowfmr, and. the only wa'y be could account for the accident wae, that they had not put in the piece of wood which should have le.en used to separate the tea side stones before they were placed in I,Rition. Deceased died directly after he was taken from under the stone—and le was removed to the Widnes Hospital. The stone which fell upon the deceased was about 10 feet Hitch,, in length, 5 feet broad, and 6 inches thick.—William Alexander said he was working with Riley when the accident happened, and lie had a very narrow escape himself of Iwing caught by the stone. Indeed, he felt the stone which killed deceased eras.- the side of one ' of his (witness's) ,rms; and it was only by the greatest goad fortune that he escaped being caught by it. Just before the accident happened the deceawd was assisting Kelly. Two side stones had been pot up and one end, ready for india rubber being Placed under them, The wedgvs had to be ni3ved in order to fli3Ce indiarubber under- neath the 'tons-c. The side stone which fell on the men had been lowered all right into its place when deeeneed went to the other end mono, and removed a thick wedge without putting inn thinner one, to keep the stone in poeition, in its place. The consequence of thin was that on moving the stone, which bad b-en properly fixed, the large one at the side immediately fell upon hitn. Riley broke the (allot the Hone upon belly by falling upon the top of him. Riley was nearly killed, and the other man very seriouely injured. lan that he had to Le removed to the hospital. Riley died in about foar minubs. The Mckle which they used was of a very good charac:er.—The Foreman &Aced that the contrac- tor ehould be recalled, and he then asked him how it watt I that when he left the work for some twenty minutes he di.l not appoint suite one. to act in his place, tad take a general euperintendence.—The Contractor said that, if possible, he avoided selecting any of the men to act as foreman over the 7:ehverr's I l'o'f a"L tilitairvh2edn ltd:l7t'Ytl'iaat"soamae ieolontc ment ought to be made by which some one wouP to left in charge of the work whenever the .ontractor was obliged to Rave it.—The Foreman said he el, eyed that Mr. Lewie, who was employcel by Shasrs. Muspratt's, M-11% pre,ent, and he should like so make an lobservation with reference to the course adopted at the works in removing any injured man to the hospital. Th, custom appeared to he to put the injured man into a kind of “ float,- which he thought most give him such a shaking in I the couree of 0 journey to the hospital that whatever little life there was in him b.fore was very likely to be knocked otc hef,e lie got . the inmitution.—Mr. Lewis said the firm ' had undertaken to ptovide a proper stretcher, similar to the Is-coot the hospital, to be used in such C.oE—Another jury- ' man said he lad noli,ed that there did not appear to bra stretch, at any of the numerous works in the town, with the exception of Mesars. GOSSAgeS.—Tte jury returned a : verdict of °Accidental death. '

Bet I , venture to think that our Mayor did not intend to show by his presence tithe meeting in question that he wae a wit.: mos for the plaintiffs in the cause of o Starr-Bowkett versus uerrnanent Building Sxieties." There a., as you are aware, several Permanent Building Societies estsblished in St. Helens, which, withont any any flourish of trumpets sr foreign aid, have, in a modest I way, done a large amout of good to the working classes of St. Helen, and with your permission, Mr. Editor, I will endeavour to show (without any attempt at electors) some of the ads-aware of the Permanent Societies over the Societies in which. Mr. Starr Admits that the principles of Permanent SoUeties are correct, but elates that they are not altiptial to the pockets of working men, who cannot avail themselves of them. In answer to this, lean point to many colliers, bricklayers joiners, and even labourers in St. Helmos who have ac- quired not only their own house, but other houses by the aid of Permanent Societies. The members for Mid-Cheshire, in , which division the Liberals have bestirred themselves in a nsanner that their Tory friends little thought them capable oh prodnee to give the present members several anxious momenta, and, finally, to enable them to participate more folly—although I think that scarcely possible—in the rural pastimes for which.by birth, education, tradition, end train- ing they ere Co eminently fitted to take a prominent and leading part. Where our political representatives hold office in her Majesty's forces it would be unreasonable to expect them to bide their diminished heads in view of the Liberal army, which has been too long compelled to march on its who; yet I do trust that the electors of Mid-Cheshire will teach our gallant oppnente one lesson in drill. and that is the e Right-about face: quick march." We in !slid-Cheshire are not weary of well-doing: and the prospect of that powi. Linty must rest with a change in the representation. It is oWy in view of their being challengei to surrengh r that the hon members deign to fsvour a portion of theelectors of the division with their views of the present state of the political atmosphere: and, with a discretion which characterimes the party, the nubjems upon which depend the happiness and prosperity of a great portion of the constituency—l mean the farmers—the tnemhers are mute J would that they all were. When they do awake to the necessities and responsi- bilitien of the position, I trust they may find in their places seen willing and competent to deal honestly and fairly with the causes which increase destitution, beggar the farmer, in- sult the intelligent county voter, and sully the fair fame of England.—Yours, AN ELECTOR tIF MID-CHESHIRE. Desth had re- sulted from compression of the brain caused by the effusion ,d blood, and the rupture of the blond vessele had been caused by the violent blow the deceased had received. Fr.elehain and neighbourhood is noted for the !very firm footing "Reebabitiam" has gained among the !better class of working men ; and I have reaaon tam believe that the Rev. H. H. illogg, M.A., the new vicar of Frodsham. intends starting a branch of the Church of England Temperance Society at once, and that it is quite likely he will have lb., co-opo-ation of the Rev.
